title: ODT termination current recycled into the array supply rail
idea: Stack: keep 40-ohm on-die termination AND add zero I/O energy. Instead of terminating DQ lines to ground or VTT through a resistor, each ODT leg returns its current into the VARY array rail through a shunt-regulated low-impedance node, so incoming write traffic tops up the rail the sense amps drain anyway; a small shunt clamp dumps only the excess.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): termination is roughly a third of DDR5 write-path power; reusing it as array supply recovers about the VARY/VDDQ fraction (~40-50%) of that energy with no protocol change.

title: Gate-charge popcount on a sub-threshold wordline ramp flags silent flips
idea: Stack: catch every retention or hammer flip AND never open the row. The sub-wordline driver ramps a row to ~0.2 V below Vth and back in 2 ns; each access transistor's gate charge depends weakly on its storage-node (source) voltage through the body effect, so a per-driver charge integrator measures the row's '1'-count without any charge transfer. A 10-bit popcount tag written with the row is compared and a mismatch triggers a targeted scrub.
why: Row hammer and refresh tail (facts 3, 9): row-level corruption is detected for ~1/100 of an activation's energy, enabling detection-driven rather than worst-case protective refresh; claimed 5-10x fewer mitigation refreshes.

title: Buried bitline's own junction becomes a millimeter-scale JFET preamp
idea: Stack: cut sense-amp offset 5x AND add no area at bitline pitch. In 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM with buried n+ bitlines, implant a lightly doped p-strip beside each bitline under the array, contacted only at the mat edges; the bitline's depletion edge modulates the strip's conductance along its whole length, so the parasitic bitline-to-substrate capacitance doubles as the gate of a giant-area JFET. True and reference strips form a differential current preamp ahead of a small latch.
why: Sensing and periphery area (facts 1, 7): mismatch scales as 1/sqrt(gate area), so a 50-100 um gate gives sub-mV offset and lets each sense amp serve ~2x more cells (~10% die area).

title: Per-die ECC-aware address permutation key replaces redundancy and fuses
idea: Stack: at most 8 bits of repair storage AND zero spare rows or columns. At sort the tester maps defects and searches 256 hard-wired XOR/rotate column-to-codeword permutations for one that puts no more than one defective cell in any on-die-ECC codeword; the 8-bit key is loaded from the SPD into a mode register, and on-die SEC silently absorbs the steered defects.
why: Periphery area and test cost (fact 7): deletes redundant rows/columns, fuse banks and compare logic (~4-6% of die) in exchange for an 8-bit key; ECC headroom is lost only in the few defect-hosting words.

title: High-equalized bitlines collect hammer electrons as the aggressor wordline falls
idea: Stack: no activation counters AND no extra refresh. Reorder precharge so that during the ~2 ns in which the aggressor wordline falls, every bitline in the mat is held at VDD instead of being equalized to VDD/2; electrons detrapped from the aggressor's gate-edge and STI interface traps then drift into the nearby positively biased bitline-contact junctions rather than the victims' storage nodes, and normal equalization follows.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the charge-pumping injection mechanism at its source with only a timing change; claimed 3-10x higher hammer threshold, so tracker tables shrink or disappear.

title: ACT-timed feed-forward charge packets replace on-die decoupling capacitors
idea: Stack: cut decap area 70% AND keep VARY droop unchanged. The command decoder knows the exact cycle each bank's sense amps fire, so a per-bank reservoir capacitor held at 2.5 V dumps a calibrated charge packet into the local VARY grid through a timed switch at that instant, cancelling droop actively; packet size is trimmed per bank from an on-die droop monitor.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): activation decap is several percent of die; a 2.5x voltage swing on a small reservoir delivers the same charge from ~1/5 of the capacitance.

title: Segmented spare rows: one spare row patches eight defective rows
idea: Stack: 75% fewer spare rows AND the same repairable defect count. Split each spare row along the existing sub-wordline-driver boundaries into eight independently remappable segments, each with its own small address match, so one physical spare row stands in for the local defective segment of up to eight different rows, since point defects rarely span a full row.
why: Redundancy share of periphery (fact 7): spare rows plus their fuses and comparators are ~2-3% of die; segment-granular sparing recovers most of it.

title: TSV copper gates an annular power transistor inside its keep-out zone
idea: Stack: use no silicon outside the TSV keep-out ring AND add bank power gating. A dedicated gate TSV runs through the stack; its liner oxide serves as the gate dielectric of a ring-shaped gate-all-around MOSFET formed by implanting source/drain rings in the otherwise dead keep-out silicon, so one TSV drive power-gates the same bank on every die of an HBM stack at once.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and idle power: turns dead keep-out area (~10% of an HBM core die) into power switches; ~100 ns gating speed is adequate for bank-level idle.

title: Open-row delta parity update removes on-die ECC read-modify-write
idea: Stack: keep on-die ECC AND never do an internal read-modify-write for masked or partial writes. With the row open, the old codeword already sits in the sense-amp latches, so a small XOR tree in the column path computes the parity change from only the overwritten bits (old XOR new) and flips the parity columns of the same open row directly in their latches within the same column cycle.
why: Bandwidth and periphery energy: DDR5 masked writes cost an extra internal column read; delta update removes it, worth ~10-20% effective write bandwidth on partial-write workloads.

title: Cell plate electrode doubles as a low-swing mat broadcast wire
idea: Stack: delete a global control-wire bundle AND add no metal. The cell plate of each mat is driven with +/-50 mV coded pulses (mat select, sense-enable timing tokens) that small comparators in the sub-wordline-driver strips decode; storage nodes are capacitively tied to the plate and simply ride along, so stored charge relative to the plate is unchanged.
why: Periphery wiring (fact 7): turns an always-present low-resistance conductor into a signal path, freeing ~5-10% of upper-metal tracks in conjunction areas.

title: Flip-minimizing write inversion for writes into an already-open row
idea: Stack: cut row-buffer write energy AND leave the external bus untouched. For each write burst into an open row, the column logic compares new data with the latched old data and stores the inverted word plus a 1-bit flag whenever that flips fewer sense-amp latches; the flag cell lives in the same row and is applied on read.
why: Energy per bit: each flipped latch swings two bitline capacitances rail to rail; inversion caps flips per word below half, trimming write restore energy ~20-30%.

title: Clocked MIM switched-capacitor resistor replaces the external ZQ resistor
idea: Stack: no precision external resistor or ZQ pin AND +/-5% driver impedance. A switched-capacitor equivalent resistor R = 1/(f*C), built from an on-die MIM capacitor clocked by CK, becomes the impedance reference; the MIM value is trimmed once at sort and tracked by the host-controlled clock frequency.
why: Periphery and package cost: removes a pin, a board component per die and the ZQ arbitration logic, which matters most in many-die stacks.

title: Stack-shared ESD lets HBM core dies drop per-TSV clamps
idea: Stack: keep handling ESD robustness AND remove full clamps from every core-die TSV I/O. Core dies carry only a tiny CDM-level clamp per TSV and are assembled with a sacrificial laser-opened shunt layer shorting all TSV columns; after bonding, the base die's full clamps protect each vertical column for every die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): per-TSV ESD devices and their spacing are a notable slice of ~2000 TSV I/O sites per core die; dropping them reclaims area and cuts TSV load capacitance ~30%.

title: Delta-coded trims: mask-ROM baseline plus tiny per-die fuse deltas
idea: Stack: shrink the fuse bank 4x AND keep per-die trims. Hard-code the product-median value of every trim (VPP, VARY, timing, references) in mask ROM and store per die only small signed deltas in a variable-length code; the boot loader adds them, since most dies sit near the median.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): e-fuse arrays and their sense latches take ~1-2% of die; entropy-coding the trims shrinks them several-fold.

title: GHz-clocked micro charge pumps embedded in every sub-wordline-driver strip
idea: Stack: no central VPP pump block AND no off-die supply. Replace the ~100 MHz central pump with hundreds of two-stage micro-pumps clocked at 2-4 GHz from the I/O clock, each with 5-10 pF of BEOL MIM inside the driver strip it feeds; flying-cap area scales as 1/f and local generation deletes the VPP distribution mesh.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): VPP pumps and capacitors are ~3-5% of die; 20x higher clocking cuts capacitor area ~10x at a modest efficiency cost.

title: Predicted mats pre-bias their wordlines just below threshold
idea: Stack: cut wordline activation charge 40% AND keep tRCD. When the scheduler queues an ACT for a mat, that mat's wordlines are lifted from the negative off level to ~0.3 V below Vth for at most 50 ns, shrinking the boosted swing the selected row and its driver must deliver; unselected rows return negative long before extra leakage matters.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): VPP charge is produced at ~30% pump efficiency, so a 40% smaller boosted swing saves ~10-15% of activate power.

title: In-DRAM row copy fills retention-test patterns in microseconds
idea: Stack: halve retention-test cost AND buy no new testers. A test mode lets the tester write one pattern row per subarray, then the die replicates it into every row by back-to-back activation copy and inverts it with a broadcast flag, collapsing each pattern fill from milliseconds over the narrow test bus to microseconds.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): multi-pattern retention tests dominate DRAM test time and tester capex; faster fills roughly double tester throughput.

title: Contact-over-active-gate layout shrinks sense-amp strip height
idea: Stack: shrink sense-amp strips 15% AND keep transistor sizes. Bring the logic-node contact-over-active-gate scheme to the sense-amp and equalizer layout: gate contacts land directly above the channel through a self-aligned cap, so the cross-coupled pair no longer needs gate extensions beyond the active area for contacts.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp strips are ~15-20% of die; removing gate-extension real estate cuts strip height ~10-15%.

title: One time-shared bank decoder serves row and column addresses
idea: Stack: halve decode transistor count AND keep random access. ACT and READ/WRITE to a bank are always separated by tRCD (>10 ns), so a single bank decoder decodes the row address, latches the one-hot result into sub-wordline-driver keepers, and is then reused for the column address with outputs steered to the column-select drivers.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): row plus column decoders are ~5-8% of die; time-sharing removes most of one of them.

title: Self-clocked single-wire internal command bus replaces parallel control routing
idea: Stack: cut bank control wiring 10x AND add no command latency beyond one cycle. Each bank's internal commands and addresses travel as a Manchester-coded serial stream on one wire at 8x the internal clock, recovered by a tiny edge-detecting deserializer at the bank, instead of dozens of parallel control and predecode lines crossing the die.
why: Periphery wiring (fact 7): control and address buses consume a large share of upper-metal tracks in the central spine; serializing them frees area and reduces switching capacitance.

title: Internal global data lines carry reads and writes simultaneously
idea: Stack: halve global data-line count AND keep read-write turnaround at zero. Each internal GIO wire is driven from both ends at once (array side for reads, I/O side for writes) and each end's receiver subtracts its own known transmitted level through a replica hybrid, so a bank streams reads outward while the next writes flow inward.
why: Periphery wiring and bandwidth (fact 7): global data lines occupy many upper-metal tracks; simultaneous bidirectional signaling halves them.

title: Voltage-ratio steering writes sub-pitch bits into a continuous ferroelectric film
idea: Collision: zero refresh demands a remanent medium, while 10x density at flat cost forbids 10x finer lithography. Keep a continuous HZO film and coarse 40 nm electrodes, and let periphery DACs set the voltage ratio on four neighbouring electrodes so the coercive-field maximum lands on any of 4x4 sub-pitch spots that a square-loop film switches alone. Reads apply the same steered field, sense the switching charge on the shared electrodes and rewrite.
why: Litho capital and refresh (facts 3, 4): 16 bits per coarse cell from electrode DACs instead of EUV; nonvolatile, so zero refresh; claimed ~10x bits per mask level.

title: Row-line Joule heating plus column field selects Curie-edge ferroelectric bits
idea: Collision: no refresh needs a remanent dipole, and flat-cost 10x density allows no access transistor. Use a ferroelectric engineered with a Curie point near 150 C, where its coercive field collapses: a 5 ns current pulse heats one row line, and only cells on that hot row switch under the moderate column voltage while cold rows ignore it. Eight such decks stack in BEOL with drivers only at tile edges.
why: Deletes access transistors and selectors (facts 2, 4): ~4F2/8 per bit with thermal coincidence replacing V/2 schemes; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Nanosecond write pulses exploit ferroelectric switching kinetics against half-select
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to ferroelectric storage, and 10x density at flat cost points to selector-free crosspoints that normally die of half-select disturb. Switching time follows Merz's law t ~ exp(alpha/E), so a 1 ns full-field pulse switches the target while half-field cells would need ~1e9x longer; drivers with sub-100 ps edges and regulated amplitude enforce the window, and a per-line disturb counter triggers rare rewrites.
why: Transistor-free FE crosspoint decks (facts 2, 4): density from 4F2 times decks with edge-only drivers; nonvolatile.

title: Sneak current through the crosspoint becomes the read reference
idea: Collision: zero refresh forces two-terminal nonvolatile cells, and flat-cost 10x density forbids per-cell selectors, so sneak paths are unavoidable. Use them as the reference: with balanced-coded data the sneak current through all unselected three-cell paths is a stable multiple of the mean cell conductance, so each column sense amp compares the selected cell's current against a scaled copy of the measured sneak current instead of a reference column.
why: Sensing in selectorless arrays (fact 7): deletes reference columns and tracks drift and temperature, enabling ~1k x 1k tiles; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Magnetoelectric bits flip only where line voltage meets package coil field
idea: Collision: no refresh calls for a magnetic state, and flat-cost density calls for no write transistors or currents. Cr2O3-type magnetoelectric antiferromagnets switch only when the product of electric and magnetic field crosses a threshold, so one package-level coil supplies a global +/-H pulse while row and column lines apply +/-V/2 and only the crossing sees the full E*H product. Reads use the exchange-coupled ferromagnet's anomalous Hall voltage on the same lines.
why: Write drivers shrink to voltage switches with no current (fact 7); crosspoint decks provide the density; nonvolatile.

title: Ultrasonic echo timing reads a whole ferroelectric row from one transducer
idea: Collision: zero refresh means remanent polarization, and 10x density means no per-column sense amp. A sub-coercive voltage step on one row makes each cell launch a piezoelectric acoustic wavelet whose phase follows its polarization sign; a single AlN transducer at the tile edge receives them in time-of-flight order (~5 um/ns), so column position becomes arrival time and one receiver decodes a 50 um row in ~10 ns without switching any cell.
why: Periphery area and destructive read (facts 7, 8): one receiver replaces hundreds of sense amps, reads are non-destructive and storage is nonvolatile.

title: Coulomb-metered write termination stretches ferroelectric endurance toward unlimited
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric storage, but 10x density at the same cost leaves no spare cells to mask fatigue. Each plate or bitline driver integrates the switching current and ends the write pulse the moment 2Pr*A of charge has moved, so no cell ever sees excess field or time, the main driver of oxygen-vacancy fatigue and imprint; cells needing abnormal charge are flagged early.
why: DRAM-class endurance in dense FE decks: removing overdrive extends cycling ~10-100x, letting 3D ferroelectric capacitors serve as working memory; nonvolatile.

title: Idle-time rejuvenation pulses reset ferroelectric fatigue tile by tile
idea: Collision: zero refresh still leaves energy for rare maintenance, while flat-cost 10x density forbids over-provisioning cells. Each tile logs its write count; during idle windows the periphery moves the tile's data to a spare tile, applies a short burst of high-field bipolar cycles that redistributes oxygen vacancies and restores remanent polarization, then moves the data back.
why: Endurance at density: in-situ fatigue recovery turns a ~1e11-cycle ferroelectric into an effectively unlimited one; nonvolatile, no refresh.

title: Antiferroelectric layers act as capacitive tier selectors in 3D ferroelectric stacks
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric storage capacitors, and 10x density at flat cost means many tiers on one vertical bitline without a transistor per tier. Put a ZrO2 antiferroelectric capacitor in series with each tier's storage capacitor: unbiased it is a small linear capacitance that blocks charge transfer, but when the tier's plate drives it past its AFE-to-FE field its capacitance jumps ~5x and couples that storage cell to the bitline.
why: Deletes per-tier access transistors and staircase decoders (facts 2, 7): capacitive selection lets 32+ tiers share one bitline; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Binary-weighted stray fields let one sensor junction read four magnets
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to nanomagnets, and 10x density points to fewer read devices than bits. Place four unwired storage nanomagnets at engineered distances above one sensor MTJ so their stray fields at the sensor are weighted 1:2:4:8; the sensor's resistance encodes all four states in one read through a 4-bit current ADC, while writes use one shared spin-orbit line per stack.
why: Read periphery and access devices per bit drop 4x (fact 7); storage magnets need no transistor or contact; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric bilayer gates switch at 0.3 V and delete charge pumps
idea: Collision: zero refresh requires remanence, and 10x density at the same cost requires the periphery to shrink rather than grow. Use rhombohedral bilayer MoS2 or hBN, whose polarization flips by interlayer sliding at ~0.3 V without domain-pinning fatigue, as the storage gate of a 2D-channel read transistor; with sub-0.5 V writes the periphery needs no VPP pumps, level shifters or thick-oxide drivers, and transferred 2D tiers stack.
why: Voltage floor and periphery area (facts 7, 10): deleting high-voltage periphery frees ~15% of die and thin tiers stack; nonvolatile.

title: Pre-poled spare rows make every ferroelectric write one-directional
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric storage, and flat-cost density chooses cheap crosspoint decks whose endurance is the weak point. The periphery keeps a pool of rows pre-poled to '0' by row-parallel plate pulses in idle time; every write goes out of place to such a row so only the '1' bits switch, and a remap table in the sense-amp strip sends the old row back to the pre-pole queue.
why: Halves switching events and write energy, removes read-before-write and doubles write speed in dense nonvolatile decks.

title: Reprogrammable ferroelectric capacitive decoders built inside the storage deck
idea: Collision: zero refresh plus flat-cost 10x density leaves no budget for CMOS decoders per deck. Build each deck's row decoder from the same ferroelectric capacitors as its cells: an address-line by row-line capacitor matrix whose polarization pattern decides which address combination couples enough charge to push a row line past its threshold-switch selector; the pattern is written at test and rewritten in the field to map out bad rows.
why: Periphery area and masks (facts 4, 7): decoders come free with the deck process and double as repair; nonvolatile.

title: Write-credit protocol trades write speed for 10x denser nonvolatile tiers
idea: Collision: zero refresh and flat-cost 10x density point to dense ferroelectric or magnetic crosspoints whose writes are slower than reads. The periphery advertises a per-bank write-credit pool over CXL; hosts spend a credit per line written and credits refill at the array's sustainable rate while reads stay DRAM-fast, so read-heavy inference (weights, KV cache) uses dense memory without a DRAM write cache.
why: Lets accelerators adopt 10x-density, zero-refresh tiers under an explicit contract instead of paying for an extra DRAM front end.

title: Polarization-vector cells store two bits read by orthogonal electrode pairs
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric remanence, and 10x density at flat cost means more bits per lithographic cell. In rhombohedral BiFeO3 the polarization takes four projected diagonal orientations, so each crosspoint gets a vertical electrode pair and a lateral electrode pair; the vertical component is read by one pair and the in-plane component by the other, giving 2 bits per cell from two binary reads rather than multilevel sensing.
why: Doubles bits per cell without analog levels; with crosspoint decks reaches 10x density; nonvolatile.

title: Mirror-poled alternate decks share lines without write disturb
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric decks, and 10x density means decks must share word and bit lines. Deposit every other deck with its electrode stack mirrored so its ferroelectric imprint points the opposite way: a write field that switches the target in deck k only pushes the sharing deck's cells further into saturation, and read pulses of opposite polarity address the upper or lower deck through the same sense amp.
why: Halves line layers and drivers per deck (facts 4, 7) while removing shared-line disturb; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Global microwave plus local voltage tuning writes magnetic crosspoint bits
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to nanomagnets, and flat-cost density points to no write transistors and no write currents. A package stripline bathes the die in a GHz field slightly off the bits' ferromagnetic resonance; the row-column voltage at one crossing shifts that bit's anisotropy through voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy into resonance, so only it absorbs enough energy to reverse.
why: Write drivers become current-free voltage switches (fact 7); crosspoint decks provide density; nonvolatile.

title: Abort-on-nucleation sensing reads ferroelectric cells without full switching
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric cells, and 10x density forbids spending energy and endurance on full destructive reads. The sense amp watches displacement current during a read ramp and kills the ramp within ~100 ps of the first switching-current onset, so a '1' cell is only nucleated, not switched, and back-switches when the field is removed; the onset itself is the data.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and endurance: roughly halves read fatigue and removes most write-back energy; nonvolatile.

title: Balanced-coded rows cancel plate switching current and shrink plate drivers
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric switching charge on every write, and 10x density at the same cost means plate drivers cannot grow with bits per row. Encode each row with a constant-weight code and write '1's and '0's in one pulse so up- and down-switching displacement currents cancel on the shared plate; the plate driver supplies only the imbalance and the linear charge.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): plate and word drivers shrink ~5-10x, the key enabler for long FE crosspoint lines; nonvolatile.

title: Compensating reverse pulses undo partial switching in half-selected cells
idea: Collision: zero refresh plus flat-cost density forces selectorless ferroelectric crosspoints, whose half-selected cells partially switch on every write. The line drivers follow each write with a short opposite-polarity half-amplitude pulse on the shared lines only, reversing sub-critical nuclei in half-selected cells while being far too weak to disturb the fully switched target.
why: Removes the half-select disturb barrier that has blocked transistor-free ferroelectric arrays since 1952, enabling dense decks; nonvolatile.

title: Anomalous Nernst readout heats one row and reads magnets as voltages
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to magnetic bits, and 10x density at the same cost forbids a tunnel junction and transistor per bit. Each bit is a nanomagnet with a Nernst-active layer (for example Co2MnGa) between a row heater line and a column sense line; a 2 ns heat pulse on one row produces a transverse anomalous Nernst voltage at each crossing whose sign gives the magnetization, read by column comparators.
why: Transistor-free, junction-free magnetic crosspoints (facts 2, 7); nonvolatile; the read path is only heaters and comparators.

title: Ice-age stochastic resonance: untrimmed comparator ensemble voting
idea: Like Milankovitch forcing that is too weak alone but paces ice ages via climate noise, each bitline feeds 16 minimum-size, deliberately untrimmed comparators whose random offsets (sigma ~30 mV) act as the noise; the count of comparators that fire encodes the sign of the ~20 mV signal, and a popcount majority gives the bit with systematic offset averaged out.
why: Removes trim fuses/calibration and lets the SA pair use near-minimum devices; targets ~30% SA-strip area cut and longer bitlines (fewer SA strips).

title: Seismic arrival-time triangulation: counter-propagating pulse-collision row select
idea: Earthquakes are located from arrival-time differences; here two pulses are launched from opposite ends of a per-mat delay ladder with a programmable launch skew, and only the stage where both pulses overlap passes an AND to its wordline driver, so the row address becomes a timing offset instead of a decoder tree.
why: Replaces the row predecoder/decoder tree (several % of die) with one delay ladder and two launch DACs per mat; ~50-70% row-decoder area cut.

title: Tidal-bore steepening: soliton-sharpened wordlines on varactor-loaded lines
idea: A tidal bore forms when a slow rising wave steepens in a shoaling river; similarly, the global wordline is loaded periodically with MOS varactors so it acts as a nonlinear transmission line where a slow, weak driver edge self-steepens into a sharp shock front at the far end.
why: Lets small drivers deliver fast far-end edges on long wordlines, shrinking sub-wordline-driver area/count ~2x and cutting tRCD spread.

title: Stratigraphic index layers: graded-threshold tier select replacing 3D staircases
idea: Geologists identify strata by signature composition; each tier of a 3D DRAM stack is deposited with a stepped channel doping (or work-function interlayer) so its select device has a distinct threshold window, and one shared vertical select line driven to level k turns on only tier k, using window comparators built in the tier stack.
why: Eliminates the staircase contact region and per-tier decoders that eat periphery area in 3D stacks; ~5-10% die area for 32+ tiers.

title: Thermoremanent magnetization: rock-style magnetic repair fuses
idea: Lava records Earth's field as it cools through its blocking temperature; repair fuses are tiny CoFe/ferrite dots on a heater line that are Joule-heated above blocking temperature and cooled in a field from a shared write strap, then read by a small magnetoresistive pickup at power-up.
why: Replaces laser fuses (large pitch, no post-package repair) and e-fuses (high-current drivers) with rewritable, low-area fuses; ~3-5x fuse-bank area cut and in-field repair.

title: Lithostatic stacking: three 1 V periphery domains stacked to native 3 V
idea: Pressure grows with depth by stacking strata; periphery logic is split into three series-stacked 1 V domains (0-1, 1-2, 2-3 V) whose currents are balanced by scheduling, so the top rail is a native ~3 V for wordline drivers without a charge pump and current is reused three times.
why: Removes most VPP charge-pump area and its ~30-40% pump efficiency loss; cuts periphery supply current ~2-3x.

title: Daisyworld homeostasis: complementary-leakage equilibrium references per mat
idea: In Daisyworld, black and white daisies with opposite temperature effects regulate the planet; each mat generates VBLP/VPLATE from a node where a population of pull-up leakage devices (current rising with temperature) balances a population of pull-down devices with matched slope, so the equilibrium voltage self-regulates with no op-amp.
why: Replaces central regulators and long reference routing with nanowatt local references; cuts regulator area and standby current ~5x.

title: Tidal locking: injection-locked mat clocks instead of a central DLL
idea: The Moon is tidally locked by a weak, persistent torque; every channel and bank group runs a tiny local ring oscillator that is injection-locked by a weak forwarded clock, so phase alignment comes from locking physics instead of a large DLL with delay lines.
why: Removes DLL area and its ~10-20 mW always-on power; faster wake from power-down.

title: Ambient-noise seismic interferometry: stimulus-free column characterization
idea: Seismologists recover Earth structure by cross-correlating ambient noise between stations; the die cross-correlates thermal noise on adjacent bitline pairs (sampled by existing SAs in a test mode) to extract each column's capacitance and coupling, with no test patterns or stimulus.
why: Per-column timing/margin maps in milliseconds at test, cutting characterization test time and guardbands ~10-20%.

title: Dendrochronology cross-dating: defect-signature dictionary compressing repair fuses
idea: Tree-ring scientists date wood by matching ring patterns to a master chronology; fail bitmaps are matched at test against a dictionary of fab defect signatures (particle cluster, scratch, bitline short), so each repair stores a short signature index plus anchor instead of full row/column addresses.
why: Cuts fuse bits per repair ~3-4x, letting more spares be used for the same fuse area and raising yield.

title: Global atmospheric circuit: distributed micro-pumps charging a shared VPP mesh
idea: Earth's ~2,000 simultaneous thunderstorms charge the ionosphere which leaks back everywhere; hundreds of tiny two-stage pumps sit in sub-wordline-driver gaps and all charge one VPP mesh, using the mesh's distributed capacitance as reservoir.
why: Removes large central pumps and VPP IR-drop guardband; ~40% pump area and lower VPP ripple.

title: Ice-core layer thinning: log-compressed row-activation history tracker
idea: Ice layers thin with depth, so old years occupy little core; a digital row-hammer tracker keeps recent activations at full resolution but merges older epochs into exponentially coarser bins (shared counters per row group), so a small SRAM covers the full refresh window.
why: Row-hammer tracking at ~1k-activation thresholds with ~4-8x less tracker SRAM than full per-row counting.

title: Braided rivers: redundant cross-linked routing of global periphery signals
idea: Braided rivers keep flowing when one channel clogs because channels split and rejoin; every critical global periphery net is routed as two or three braided parallel wires with periodic cross-links, so single opens or via failures no longer kill the die.
why: Raises periphery yield (periphery is ~49% of die and holds many single-point nets) by a few % with no fuses.

title: Earthquake early warning: P-wave droop detection throttling activations
idea: Early-warning systems act on the fast P-wave before the destructive S-wave; a fast droop detector at each pump output detects VPP/VARY sag and briefly delays queued ACT commands to far banks before the droop propagates, so supplies are sized for average not worst-case burst.
why: Allows ~30% smaller pump/decap reservoirs and tighter tFAW-type limits.

title: Telegraph earth return: single-wire global datalines over a buried return plane
idea: Early telegraphs used the Earth as the return conductor to halve wire count; global I/O lines become single-ended over a buried low-impedance return plane (backside power-rail metal), replacing differential GIO pairs.
why: Halves global dataline tracks in the periphery and column-path area; ~2-4% die area.

title: Tidal harmonic analysis: feedforward replay of periodic supply disturbances
idea: Tide prediction sums known harmonic constituents; the VPP/VARY regulators learn the periodic disturbance waveforms tied to refresh cadence and command patterns and inject a pre-recorded correction current in sync, leaving feedback to handle only the residual.
why: Cuts regulator bandwidth and decap needs ~2x for the periodic part of the load.

title: Thermophile enzymes: zero-temperature-coefficient biased sense amplifiers
idea: Hyperthermophile enzymes keep activity flat across temperatures; SA enable/tail devices are biased at the gate voltage where mobility and threshold drift cancel (the ZTC point), making sensing speed and offset nearly temperature-independent.
why: Removes temperature guardbands in tRCD and SA margin (~10-15%) enabling longer bitlines or lower VARY.

title: Halophile isosmotic balance: iso-potential parking of idle wordline-driver nodes
idea: Salt-in halophiles avoid osmotic stress by matching inside and outside concentrations; in standby, all nodes of each idle wordline-driver and decoder stage are parked at the same potential so no device has a drain-source or GIDL-driving drop.
why: Cuts periphery standby leakage (dominant in large VPP drivers) ~5-10x without full power gating latency.

title: Heap leaching of low-grade ore: periphery-slow dies as relaxed-timing tier
idea: Miners profit from low-grade ore by cheap bulk processing; dies that fail spec only because of slow sense amps or decoders are binned into a relaxed-timing CXL capacity product whose controller uses longer tRCD/tRAS, instead of scrapping them.
why: Recovers several % of wafer output as sellable bits; raises usable supply without new capacity.

title: Crack-seal veins: self-healing periphery interconnect with liquid-metal capsules
idea: Rock fractures heal as hydrothermal fluid precipitates minerals in the crack; global periphery wires are embedded with microcapsules of Ga-In eutectic that rupture at a crack or electromigration void and wick in to restore conduction.
why: Raises periphery reliability/yield and allows narrower global wires; speculative few-% yield gain.

title: Tardigrade vitrification: unpowered sense amps holding open pages on bitlines
idea: Tardigrades survive by vitrifying their state and halting metabolism; after a row is restored, both SA tails are switched off and the full-rail bitlines themselves hold the open page as a frozen dynamic state, with the SA re-enabled only for a brief re-latch before each column access.
why: Cuts SA static/leakage power during long open-page periods ~5-10x.

title: Lightning arresters: micro spark-gap ESD at DRAM I/O pads
idea: Power lines survive lightning with gas-discharge arresters; each I/O pad gets a sealed 1-2 um gas micro-gap (sacrificial-oxide cavity, i-line litho, 0.35 um rules) that breaks down at ~10 V during ESD, replacing most of the large diode/clamp stack.
why: Cuts pad capacitance ~0.5-1 pF and ESD area; lower I/O energy per bit (CV^2) and faster DQ.

title: Karst aquifers: porous anodic-alumina reservoirs for pumped-storage VPP
idea: Karst rock stores huge water volume in dissolved pores; a package-level aluminum layer is anodized (1990s chemistry, no litho) into 10-um-deep porous alumina, coated with ALD/sputtered electrode, and used as a dense VPP reservoir charged during idle and drained during activation bursts.
why: Lets the on-die pump be sized for average rather than peak current; ~50% pump area cut.

title: Thermoluminescence traps: hot-carrier charge-trap OTP repair fuses
idea: Minerals store radiation dose as trapped charge read out by heating; repair bits are written by hot-carrier injection into the gate oxide of standard thick-oxide 180-250 nm periphery transistors, shifting threshold ~0.5 V, and sensed by a simple differential pair at power-up.
why: Eliminates laser-fuse pitch and e-fuse high-current drivers with no extra masks; ~5x fuse area cut and post-package repair.

title: Carbonate pH buffer: capacitance-peaked decoupling pinning the bitline precharge rail
idea: Seawater's carbonate system resists pH change most strongly at its pKa; the VBLP rail is decoupled with MOS capacitors whose flat-band is implanted so their capacitance peaks exactly at VARY/2, giving maximum stiffness where the rail must sit (built at 250 nm rules).
why: Shrinks VBLP regulator and decap area ~2x for the same precharge accuracy.

title: Seismic P and S waves: phantom-mode signaling on global/package lines
idea: One rock carries compressional and shear waves at once; two differential pairs also carry a third signal as the common-mode difference between pairs (telephone phantom circuit), using 180 nm-pitch wires and centre-tapped drivers.
why: 1.5x data per wire for global I/O and package lanes, cutting periphery routing area or ball count ~33%.

title: Seismic tomography: coded multi-row leakage group testing on legacy testers
idea: Tomography reconstructs Earth from many summed ray paths; the tester opens coded sets of rows and measures summed bitline leakage with a 1990s parametric unit, then solves a group-testing inverse to locate weak cells in O(log N) measurements.
why: Cuts retention/weak-cell test time ~10x on cheap old testers, lowering test cost per bit.

title: Pompeii worm thermal gradient: etched thermal moat between periphery and array
idea: The Pompeii worm lives with its tail at 80 C and head at 22 C; a backside KOH-etched trench (1990s MEMS tool) and separate heat-spreader paths keep hot periphery (pumps, I/O) thermally isolated from the array, holding the array ~10-15 C cooler.
why: Halves cell leakage via temperature, cutting refresh power ~2x without new refresh logic.

title: River-basin channel networks: optimal-channel power grid in thick top metal
idea: River basins self-organize into networks that minimize energy dissipation; the periphery power grid is laid out as a computed optimal channel network in 2-3 um thick 1990s Al top metal instead of a uniform mesh.
why: Frees one fine metal layer or ~30% of power-grid tracks for signals at equal IR drop.

title: Lake seiches: standing-wave clock distribution on coarse transmission lines
idea: Lakes slosh in standing waves with uniform phase across each half basin; the command/clock spine is a 180 nm-rule resonant line excited at a standing-wave mode so all taps see equal phase with no H-tree buffers.
why: Cuts clock-tree power ~50% and skew without DLL/buffer chains.

title: Seismometer JFET preamps: junction-gated FET sense amplifier pairs
idea: Broadband seismometer front ends use JFETs for low 1/f and random-telegraph noise; the SA input pair is a junction-gated FET (no gate oxide traps) built with 1990s implant steps, lowering noise and offset drift.
why: Reduces required bitline signal ~30%, enabling longer bitlines and fewer SA strips.

title: Tourmaline permanent dipole: electret-referenced bitline reference voltage
idea: Tourmaline carries a permanent electric polarization; a corona-charged SiO2/Si3N4 electret (1990s microphone process) coupled to a reference electrode provides a fixed, supply-free reference for the precharge/reference node.
why: Removes a reference generator and its standby current; ~1-2% periphery area.

title: Volcanic zeolite: porous mineral low-k dielectric for periphery global wires
idea: Zeolites formed from volcanic ash are crystalline and highly porous; spin-on pure-silica zeolite films (k~2.0, mechanically stiffer than amorphous porous oxides) insulate 250 nm-pitch global periphery wires.
why: Cuts global-wire capacitance ~40%, lowering on-die data-movement energy and driver sizes.

title: Tsunami shoaling: tapered-impedance package traces giving passive receiver gain
idea: Tsunamis grow taller as water shallows; package traces taper from low to high impedance (coarse 1990s substrate rules) so a small-swing driver arrives at the high-impedance receiver with ~1.5-2x voltage gain.
why: Lowers driver swing and I/O energy per bit ~40% for short links.

title: Vibroseis chirp correlation: low-amplitude TSV defect inspection
idea: Vibroseis trucks send long low-amplitude chirps and correlate to get sharp echoes; the HBM base die injects a chirp into each TSV via 180 nm-rule test circuitry and correlates the reflection to find voids or resistive joints before stacking.
why: Catches bad TSVs early, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss.

title: Mangrove forests: resistive-snubber decaps damping supply resonance
idea: Mangroves damp tsunamis by dissipating energy rather than reflecting it; a fraction of periphery decaps are built with deliberate series resistance (250 nm poly resistors) tuned to critically damp the package-die LC resonance.
why: Removes resonance peaks so total decap area can drop ~30%.

title: St. Elmo's fire point discharge: nanogap vacuum-channel wordline drivers
idea: Sharp masts concentrate fields until they emit; vertical field-emission micro-triodes whose 50 nm gap is set by a sacrificial film thickness (not litho, so 1990s tools suffice) switch the 3 V wordline rail with tiny area and no oxide reliability limits.
why: Speculative: shrinks high-voltage driver area and removes thick-oxide device needs.

title: Rogue-wave dispersive focusing: chirp-compressed wordline select
idea: Rogue waves form where dispersion focuses many waves into one spot; a chirped pulse sent into a dispersive RC/LC ladder (180 nm rules) compresses to a peak at a position set by chirp rate, and only the row where the peak exceeds threshold fires.
why: Replaces row decoder trees with one chirp generator per mat; large decoder-area cut if timing control holds.

title: Geodes: sacrificial-cavity coaxial shields around global periphery wires
idea: Geodes are hollow shells lined inward; global clock/data wires at 250 nm rules are wrapped in a sacrificial-oxide-released cavity and a grounded metal shell, forming on-die coax with low capacitance and near-zero crosstalk.
why: Allows denser, lower-energy global routing in the periphery; ~30-50% wire capacitance and crosstalk cut.

title: Petrified wood pseudomorphs: fully silicided contact plugs replacing tungsten
idea: Petrified wood keeps its shape as silica replaces cellulose atom by atom; periphery contact plugs are patterned as polysilicon at 0.25 um and fully converted in place to NiSi/CoSi2, removing tungsten CVD.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) from periphery contacts and WF6 chemistry.

title: Tree-trunk annular growth: deposition-defined vertical surround-gate periphery transistors
idea: Trees add girth in annular rings; periphery transistors are etched pillars wrapped by a surround gate, with channel length set by deposited film thickness rather than litho, so 1990s steppers give short-channel performance.
why: Gives sub-100 nm gate length with 180 nm tools; ~2-3x periphery transistor density.

title: Ocean acoustic thermometry: delay-line temperature sensing on existing global wires
idea: Ocean basin temperature is measured from sound travel time; the die measures propagation delay along an existing long global wire to infer the average temperature of each region, using 180 nm-rule counters.
why: Removes dedicated thermal sensors and adapts driver/pump bias per region; small area and power saving.

title: Plate strips as second bitline: the ground becomes the signal
idea: Paradox: the 'quiet' common plate is made a signal wire. Pattern the capacitor top plate into strips aligned with each bitline and let the strip float during read, so the cell charge produces equal and opposite swings on its bitline and on its own plate strip; the sense amp compares BL against that strip instead of a reference bitline, and strips are re-tied to VPL after restore.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and sense margin: ~1.5-1.8x differential from the same ~5 fF cell, spendable as a lower-aspect-ratio capacitor or longer bitlines (fewer SA stripes, periphery area -10-15%).

title: Decision-feedback global data lines turn interference into known information
idea: Paradox: inter-symbol interference is treated as known data rather than noise. Long, unrepeated, minimum-pitch global I/O lines are driven at full rate and each global sense amp subtracts the predicted residue of the previous 1-2 bits with a one-tap current-steering decision-feedback equalizer before latching, so lines need settle only ~40% per bit.
why: Periphery routing (fact 7) and data-movement energy (fact 5): removes repeaters and wide spacing on global buses, ~2x usable line length or ~30% less global-route area and ~25% lower bus energy.

title: Cell-capacitor threshold-logic row decoders
idea: Paradox: the element that stores data is made to compute addresses. Each local row decoder is a capacitive threshold gate: binary-weighted groups of the array's own pillar capacitors are wired to the true or complement address line per that row's code and couple onto one inverter input, so only an exact match reaches the full-sum trip point; built in the existing edge dummy-cell zone with no added masks.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): replaces 10-20-transistor NAND trees per decoder with one inverter plus capacitors printed at cell density, ~30-50% smaller row-decoder area.

title: Pulse-collision decoder: two travelling pulses meet at one row
idea: Paradox: a signal present everywhere selects exactly one place. Two short pulses are launched from opposite ends of a shared tapped delay line running past the local wordline drivers; a driver fires only where both pulses overlap (sum above its threshold), and the collision point, set by the relative launch delay from a small timing DAC, picks one of 8-16 local rows.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): replaces the final local-decode stage and its predecode wiring with 2 lines plus a timing DAC, ~40% less local-decoder area if delay spread is held within one row slot.

title: Walsh-coded global data lines that thrive on deliberate collisions
idea: Paradox: many mats talk on one wire at the same time and are still understood. Each mat spreads its output bit over 8 chips with its own orthogonal Walsh code onto a shared, unshielded global line; a correlator at the bank edge despreads all mats in parallel, and the processing gain lets each chip run at ~20-30 mV amid neighbor crosstalk.
why: Periphery routing and data-movement energy (facts 5, 7): drops shields and spacing (~40% less global-route area) and allows sub-50 mV signaling, ~3x lower global I/O energy at equal aggregate throughput.

title: Sip-read: take a fifth of the charge, skip the restore
idea: Paradox: a destructive read made non-destructive by being stingy. A sub-nanosecond, low-overdrive wordline pulse lets only ~20% of the cell charge onto the bitline, an isolated latch resolves it without swinging the bitline, and the cell keeps ~80% of its charge; a 2-bit per-row sip counter forces a real full-swing restore only after 2-3 sips or at the next refresh.
why: Destructive read and overfetch energy (fact 8) plus row hammer (fact 9): most reads avoid full bitline swing (~2-3x lower read energy) and far fewer full-swing activations feed hammer disturb.

title: Voltage-stacked wordline domain whose return current powers the logic
idea: Paradox: the high-voltage rail is placed in series with the logic so its 'waste' current is the logic's supply. Wordline drivers live in a floating domain stacked on top of the periphery logic domain; charge used to raise wordlines returns through the logic domain instead of to ground, and a small push-pull balancer absorbs mismatch, replacing the VPP charge pump.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): on-die VPP pumps run ~25-35% efficient; stacking delivers wordline charge at ~85-90%, roughly halving wordline energy and removing pump area and its decap (~3-5% die).

title: Error-correcting address codes make sloppy row decoders exact
idea: Paradox: adding redundancy shrinks the periphery. Row addresses are broadcast as a distance-3 constant-weight code on the predecode lines and every local decoder is a k-of-n threshold gate, so the correct row still fires (and no second row fires) when any single predecode line is stuck, weak or slow; decoders can then use near-minimum devices and laxer process windows.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and yield: removes most decoder guardband and decode-path redundancy, ~20-30% smaller row decoders and ~2-4% higher die yield.

title: Self-held floating wordlines let one decoder serve four banks
idea: Paradox: a wordline disconnected from its driver that stays on. After the decoder raises a wordline it is isolated and holds VPP on its own ~200 fF capacitance (plus a tiny keeper) for tRAS, freeing the same decoder and driver to fire a row in the next interleaved bank; one decoder/driver column is time-multiplexed across 4 banks.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): row decoder and driver stripes (~10-12% of die) shrink ~3-4x for ~7-9% die area saved; bitline-coupling droop on the floating line is bounded to ~0.1 V by design.

title: Trap-programmed analog address levels replace predecode trees
idea: Paradox: an analog voltage carries a digital address exactly. A few address wires per mat carry 8-16-level voltages; each wordline driver's input pair has charge-trap-programmed thresholds forming a window comparator that conducts only at its own level, programmed once at wafer test with a high-voltage pulse.
why: Periphery (fact 7): collapses log2(N) predecode wires and NAND stages into ~2-3 analog lines per mat, ~30% less row-decode area and wiring.

title: Periphery built from thousands of identical vertical array transistors
idea: Paradox: the crudest, most variable device becomes a precision analog part by sheer multiplicity. In a 4F2 vertical-channel array, sense amps, drivers and decoders are built from parallel banks of the very same vertical access transistors printed at array pitch (e.g. 64 in parallel per SA input device), so mismatch averages by sqrt(N) and periphery reuses the array patterning instead of separate planar-CMOS modules.
why: Capital and litho (fact 4) plus periphery (fact 7): removes ~5-8 periphery-only gate/implant masks and lets periphery shrink with the array pitch.

title: Hot periphery island, cold array: one die, two climates
idea: Paradox: one die deliberately runs hot and cold at once. Heat-producing periphery (I/O, pumps, control) is grouped into an island ringed by deep oxide-filled thermal trenches and a thinned silicon bridge, run near 110 C with low-Vt fast devices, while the array has its own heat path to the lid and runs ~15-20 C cooler.
why: Retention vs periphery speed: retention roughly halves per ~10 C, so a 15-20 C cooler array gives ~3x retention, while the hot island tolerates low-Vt devices for ~20% faster or smaller logic.

title: Vacuum-gap field-emission transistors as wordline drivers
idea: Paradox: emptiness is the conductor. Wordline drivers use nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (sharp TiN or Si emitter tips 30-50 nm from a collector, gated in-plane) that switch 3-5 V with no gate-oxide reliability limit, because electrons cross the gap ballistically instead of through a stressed dielectric.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and periphery: high-voltage wordline drivers are large thick-oxide devices; vacuum devices could shrink driver stripes ~3x and eliminate the thick-oxide module.

title: Surface acoustic wave packets select mats by strain
idea: Paradox: sound picks out electrons. A thin ScAlN transducer at each bank edge launches a micrometre-scale surface-acoustic-wave packet across the mats; strain-gated (piezoresistive) mat-enable switches conduct only where the packet sits when the global enable pulses, so mat and segment selection is set by launch timing instead of global decode logic.
why: Periphery (fact 7): replaces global mat-select decoders and their wiring with one transducer per bank, speculative ~30% cut in global decode area.

title: Pseudo-random bitline twists whiten pattern coupling noise
idea: Paradox: disorder improves margin. Instead of the classic 1-3 regular twists, bitline pairs twist at pseudo-random segment boundaries drawn from a de Bruijn-style schedule, so each bitline's coupling from any neighbor sums over many uncorrelated segments and worst-case data-pattern noise falls roughly as 1/sqrt(segments).
why: Sense margin (facts 1, 8): recovers ~10-20 mV of worst-case coupling, worth ~15-25% more cells per bitline (fewer SA stripes) or a shorter capacitor.

title: Wordlines double as heaters that anneal leakage-tail traps
idea: Paradox: heat, retention's enemy, is used to cure retention. In a maintenance mode, a block's data is migrated out and both ends of selected buried wordlines are driven to pass ~1 mA, Joule-heating the access-transistor region to ~300-400 C for milliseconds to anneal the interface traps behind GIDL and VRT tail cells, then data returns.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): pruning the worst tail cells could extend the guaranteed retention window ~2x and heal field-degraded rows (precedent: self-healing heaters in flash).

title: Deliberately blown cell capacitors replace the e-fuse bank
idea: Paradox: breaking a volatile cell creates permanent memory. A reserved row of ordinary array cells stores trim and redundancy bits by test-mode overvoltage breakdown of the high-k capacitor dielectric; at power-up the plate is raised and blown cells, now shorted to plate, read as hard 1s through the normal sense amps into latches.
why: Periphery (fact 7): e-fuse/laser-fuse banks with their program and latch circuits take ~2-4% of die; storing the bits at 6F2 shrinks that ~10x with no added masks.

title: Cell plate's microfarads become the chip's ESD shock absorber
idea: Paradox: the most fragile structure protects the chip. The common capacitor plate, which through billions of cells presents microfarad-class capacitance to the substrate, is linked to each pad's ESD rail by a small trigger diode so an ESD pulse's charge dumps into the plate (rising only ~0.1-0.3 V) instead of into large clamp devices.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and I/O energy: ESD clamps beside 100+ pads use ~2-3% of die; shrinking them 3-5x also cuts pad capacitance and I/O switching energy.

title: Sacrificial test periphery placed in the scribe line
idea: Paradox: circuits built in order to be destroyed. BIST engines, test-mode decoders, probe-only pads and fuse-programming drivers are placed in the kerf between dies and linked through breakable straps; after wafer sort and fuse programming the dicing saw removes them, leaving only thin isolation at the die edge.
why: Periphery (fact 7): test-only circuitry is ~4-8% of die area; moving it into otherwise wasted kerf yields ~5% more dies per wafer with no added process.

title: Rotated 3D tiers where every line both selects and senses
idea: Paradox: one wire is both a wordline and a bitline. In a stacked 3D array, tiers alternate 90 degrees so the metal plane between tier k and k+1 serves as bitlines for tier k and as gate lines for tier k+1; only one tier is active at a time and the staircase periphery switches each line between a sense amp and a wordline driver.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2) and periphery: halves line planes and staircase contacts per tier pair (~40% fewer steps) and lets two tiers share one periphery strip.

title: Shaped wordline falling edges raise the row-hammer threshold
idea: Paradox: a slower edge makes the memory faster. Wordline drivers use a two-slope, current-starved falling edge (fast down to about Vt, then a ~2 ns controlled tail) so channel electrons drain back to the bitline instead of being injected toward neighboring storage nodes, reducing disturb charge per activation.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): a 2-4x cut in per-activation disturb raises the hammer threshold proportionally, removing much mitigation refresh (~5-10% bandwidth/energy) for ~0.5 ns of tRP.
